record.title: A paper reports a nonlinear difficulty scale that changes interpretation of METR time horizons for short software tasks
record.summary: Nguyen and Fithian reanalyze METR’s public Time Horizon 1.1 data for 228 software-engineering tasks and 26 AIs using shared-slope logistic, monotone-spline and item-response models. Their preprint reports that task difficulty is nearly flat against human completion time from 2–30 minutes, so the same 10× increase in a displayed time horizon can represent different changes in task difficulty across regions. Under five-fold cross-validation across 79 task families, their proposed models reportedly outperform the selected shared-slope baseline on all 12 proper-scoring metrics; most of the gain comes from estimates in the 2–15 minute band. They do not challenge the exponential trend itself. This is a single author-reported analysis of one public software-task suite, not an independent reproduction or evidence that the metric fails outside the analyzed interval. METR’s own January Time Horizon 1.1 note says the suite was revised from 170 to 228 tasks and reports a different post-2023 doubling estimate under the new suite, while warning that the compared model sets overlap but are not identical and that task composition affects the quantity measured; this is context, not a reproduction of the preprint’s nonlinear fit.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that the mapping from human time to latent task difficulty is nearly flat for tasks assigned 2–30 minutes, making equal time-horizon multipliers non-comparable across that region and other regions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that their spline and item-response estimates outperform a shared-slope logistic baseline on all 12 displayed proper-scoring metrics under five-fold cross-validation by task family; most gains come from short horizons.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors state that release dates are not used in fitting and that they do not challenge the observed exponential growth in the displayed time horizons.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: METR’s own Time Horizon 1.1 announcement says the suite changed from 170 to 228 tasks (73 added, 15 removed, 53 updated) and reports a 131-day post-2023 doubling estimate under TH1.1 versus 165 days under TH1 for mostly overlapping but non-identical model sets; METR attributes the difference to shifts in older and newer model estimates and notes task-distribution sensitivity. This is context about the benchmark revision, not an independent reproduction of the new paper’s nonlinear analysis.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent implementation has reproduced the spline/item-response fits and 12-metric cross-validation results.
The analysis is limited to METR’s software-engineering task suite and does not validate time-horizon annotations for other domains or future longer-task suites.
No author code repository was located in the paper or bounded source check; the paper describes methods but reproducibility still requires implementation.

brief.importance_rationale: If valid beyond this analyzed benchmark, the result changes how researchers interpret widely used software-task time-horizon estimates and comparable benchmark extensions. Its consequence is notable for capability measurement, while the reported nonlinear region is localized and the analysis remains a single unreproduced preprint on one task suite.
limitations: The results are reported in a single arXiv v1 preprint and have not been independently reproduced in this activation.
The analysis uses one software-engineering benchmark suite and does not establish generality to other capability domains.
Twenty-nine percent of task human-time annotations use expert estimates because direct human timing was unavailable or judged invalid.
Most reported differences are localized to tasks with assigned human times of roughly 2–30 minutes; the authors do not challenge the exponential trend itself.

The scoring results do not establish that human time is a valid annotation for all tasks; the authors assume several earlier construct-validity questions and focus their diagnostics on predictiveness and comparability.
No code repository was located during this check.

technical.claimed_result: On 228 tasks and 26 AIs, the authors report a nonlinear human-time-to-task-difficulty mapping that is nearly flat in the 2–30 minute region. Their proposed estimates reportedly dominate their selected baseline on all 12 displayed proper-scoring metrics; the largest estimate differences and most metric gains occur for 2–15 minute horizons.
technical.demonstrated_result: The v1 preprint and analysis are publicly accessible, and METR’s underlying task data are described as public. This activation inspected the abstract, methods, results and discussion but did not rerun the analysis or independently verify the scoring results.
technical.mechanism: The authors fit alternative success-versus-human-time curves with a shared-slope logistic baseline, a monotone spline model and an item-response model. They compare estimates using five-fold cross-validation split by task family, crossed with proper scoring rules and three task/family weighting schemes, and add diagnostics for predictiveness and comparability.
technical.regime: METR Time Horizon 1.1 software-engineering task suite: 228 tasks, 79 task families and 26 AI systems; human-time annotations include expert-assigned values for 29% of tasks whose human timing was unavailable or judged invalid. Evaluations use five-fold task-family cross-validation.
technical.reproducibility: The preprint describes the models and evaluation; it states that METR’s data are public. No author code repository was located during this check, and no independent implementation or reproduction was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: The authors compare against METR’s original log-linear logistic specification and a shared-slope logistic baseline, which they select based on prior work and their own reported cross-validation. Their Models 1 and 2 reportedly outperform the shared-slope baseline across all 12 proper-scoring metrics. METR’s first-party TH1.1 announcement documents the suite revision (170 to 228 tasks) and reports a 131-day versus 165-day post-2023 doubling estimate across mostly overlapping, non-identical model sets; METR attributes the shift partly to task composition and revised model estimates.

brief.title: A paper reports a nonlinear difficulty scale that changes interpretation of METR time horizons for short software tasks
brief.why_it_matters: Time-horizon estimates are used to communicate AI software-task capability and may inform benchmark design and policy discussion. If the paper’s analysis holds, raw equal-multiplier jumps in the 2–30 minute region are not comparable to jumps elsewhere; reporting success curves and task-to-difficulty diagnostics would make the measure easier to interpret. The paper leaves the overall exponential trend intact and does not establish external validity beyond this task suite.
